The French angelfish Pomacanthus paru exhibits a life history strategy typical of large-bodied coral reef pomacanthids, with significant investment in early growth. Newly hatched larvae emerge from small, pelagic eggs; the wet weight at birth is estimated at 0.00011 grams [Wwb = 0.00011 grams], a value consistent with an assumed egg diameter of approximately 0.6 mm, which is smaller than the 0.9 mm diameter reported for the congener Pomacanthus annularis. Following a pelagic larval phase lasting several weeks, metamorphosing individuals settle onto reef habitats and begin a period of rapid juvenile growth. Field surveys and otolith-based back-calculation studies indicate that this species reaches a maximum adult standard length of 41.1 centimeters [Li = 41.1 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger angelfish in the tropical western Atlantic. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, derived from length-weight regressions, reaches 1933 grams [Wwi = 1933 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic tissue required to support a long-lived, iteroparous adult existence on structurally complex reef environments.

Sexual maturation in Pomacanthus paru is a comparatively protracted process, with puberty occurring after several years of sustained growth. Morphological and histological examination of gonadal tissue from wild-caught specimens has established that the standard length at puberty is 23.3 centimeters [Lp = 23.3 centimeters]. At this length, individuals have accumulated sufficient body mass to support the energetic demands of gametogenesis; the corresponding wet weight at puberty is 370.6 grams [Wwp = 370.6 grams], marking a clear threshold in the transition from somatic growth to reproductive allocation. This length-based maturation schedule is comparable to that observed in other large pomacanthids, where puberty is typically attained when individuals reach approximately fifty to sixty percent of their asymptotic length. The delay in maturation allows French angelfish to achieve a body size that reduces vulnerability to gape-limited predators and enhances competitive ability for high-quality shelter sites and feeding territories on the reef.

Reproductive output in French angelfish is characterized by the production of numerous small pelagic eggs during each spawning event. Under the stable thermal conditions typical of their tropical reef habitat, with water temperatures averaging 26.6 °C [T = 26.6 °C], females release approximately 1507 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1507 eggs per spawning event] and spawn multiple times across the breeding season, for an estimated annual rate of 2 spawning events per year [F_R_i = 2 spawning events per year]. This elevated fecundity likely reflects an evolutionary trade-off where high egg production compensates for substantial losses during the pelagic larval phase, as only a minute fraction of ichthyoplankton survives to settlement. The reproductive strategy of Pomacanthus paru is therefore one of high fecundity and low per-offspring investment, consistent with the classic r-selected end of the life history continuum within a generally K-selected family.

Longevity data for the French angelfish suggest a remarkably extended lifespan for a reef teleost. Investigations of individuals maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 26.6 °C [T = 26.6 °C] have documented a maximum lifespan of 27 years [am = 27 years], with some wild-caught specimens exhibiting otolith annuli consistent with comparable ages. This impressive longevity exceeds the estimates for many similarly sized reef fishes and is thought to be facilitated by the species' robust body armor, relatively low natural predation rates, and a diet that includes sponges and other benthic invertebrates that are consistently available across seasons. The prolonged reproductive window afforded by such a lifespan allows iteroparous females to buffer against years of poor recruitment, maintaining population stability over decadal timescales. Such a life history strategy is particularly advantageous in stable, species-rich coral reef environments where competition for space and resources is intense.

Comparative life history analyses across Western Atlantic pomacanthids reveal that the growth parameters and reproductive timing of Pomacanthus paru align closely with those of its congener P. arcuatus, although significant divergences are evident in ultimate body size. While the maximum standard length of 41.1 centimeters [Li = 41.1 centimeters] recorded for P. paru is comparable, its ultimate wet weight of 1933 grams [Wwi = 1933 grams] is somewhat reduced relative to predictions based on asymptotic length alone, suggesting a slightly more slender body morphology. The standard length at puberty of 23.3 centimeters [Lp = 23.3 centimeters] and the associated wet weight at puberty of 370.6 grams [Wwp = 370.6 grams] provide a clear benchmark for differentiating juvenile and adult life stages in field studies. These morphometric relationships were derived from length-weight regressions applied to a large sample of individuals spanning the full size range of the species, ensuring robust estimates for ecological and fisheries management applications.
